title: Relational databases and when SQL is right
scopeHtml: Scope: when SQL fits, schema design and normalisation, primary keys at scale, connection pooling with numbers, scaling reads, safe migrations.

notes.title: What a relational database gives you
notes.html:
A relational database stores data in tables (rows and columns), links tables with keys, and lets you ask questions in SQL while promising that your data stays correct. The big promises are: a fixed schema, joins, constraints (a foreign key cannot point to nothing), and transactions (covered in a later note).

Why it is the default choice: the data is usually relational anyway (users have orders, orders have items), the query planner figures out how to answer ad-hoc questions, and 40+ years of tooling exist. Postgres and MySQL on one good machine handle far more than most startups ever need.

Worked example. A 64-core, 256 GB Postgres box with NVMe disks can serve roughly 20,000 to 50,000 simple indexed reads per second and 5,000 to 15,000 transactional writes per second (very workload dependent; always benchmark). A shop with 5M orders a year, about 0.16 orders/s on average, is nowhere near the limit.

Industry examples. Instagram ran on Postgres for years and sharded it only when needed. Stripe runs its core ledger on sharded MongoDB-style infra but uses strong consistency guarantees everywhere money moves. Shopify ran a huge MySQL fleet sharded by shop ("pods"). Stack Overflow served billions of page views from a few SQL Server machines.

Everyday analogy. A well-organised filing cabinet with a librarian (the planner) who decides the fastest way to find your folder, and rules that stop anyone filing a page under a customer that does not exist.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "SQL does not scale". Single-node SQL scales a lot; sharding it is the hard, late step.
  • Picking NoSQL "because scale" with no number to justify it.
  • Forgetting that the choice is partly about queries: if you do not know your access patterns yet, SQL is the safer bet.

notes.title: When SQL is the right choice
notes.html:
Choose SQL when you need correctness across several rows or tables, flexible queries, or you do not know the future queries yet. Typical fits: payments, orders, inventory, bookings, user accounts, anything with money or stock counts.

Choose something else when: the data is a giant append-only stream (use a log or wide-column store), you need sub-millisecond key lookups at millions of ops/s (key-value), or the data is truly a graph with deep traversals.

Need SQL fits? Why
Money transfer between two accounts Yes Multi-row ACID transaction
Ad-hoc reports and joins Yes Planner handles unknown queries
1M writes/s of sensor points Not alone Single-node write ceiling; use LSM/time-series
Session lookup by ID at 500k/s Overkill Redis is cheaper per op
Friends-of-friends depth 5 Poor Many self-joins explode

Decision gravity. Choosing the primary store is close to a one-way door: moving 2 TB of live data between engines takes months (dual writes, backfill, verification). Choosing SQL first and adding a cache or search index later is reversible, because those are derived copies.

Industry examples. Uber's early trip store was Postgres, later moved to a custom MySQL-based "Schemaless" layer when write scale and sharding needs grew. Airbnb, GitHub and Shopify all stay on MySQL with heavy sharding rather than leave SQL.

Everyday analogy. A spreadsheet with strict column rules is great for accounting. It is the wrong tool for a stream of 100,000 sensor readings a second.

Common interview traps.

  • Using SQL as a queue (polling SELECT ... WHERE status='NEW'); use a real queue or SKIP LOCKED carefully.
  • Storing large blobs (images) in rows; keep them in object storage and store the URL.

notes.title: Schema design basics and normalisation
notes.html:
Normalisation means storing each fact once. If a customer's address is copied into every order row, changing it means updating thousands of rows and risking inconsistencies. So you put customers in one table and reference them by ID.

The rules in plain words:

  • 1NF: every cell holds one value, no comma-separated lists.
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole key.
  • 3NF: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on each other.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total_cents BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Notes on choices: money as integer cents (never floats); TIMESTAMPTZ not local time; a foreign key index is not automatic in Postgres, you must create it yourself or deletes on the parent scan the child table.

Worked example. 10M orders, each with a duplicated 200-byte address: 2 GB wasted, plus an address change touching up to dozens of rows per customer. Normalised, the address is one 200-byte row.

Industry examples. Most OLTP systems at Stripe, Shopify and GitHub are normalised to 3NF in the core, with deliberate denormalised read tables for hot paths.

Everyday analogy. A contact book where each person is written once and the party invite list just points to names, rather than rewriting everyone's phone number on every invite.

Common interview traps.

  • Floats for money.
  • Storing arrays or JSON in a column and then needing to query inside it constantly.
  • Using natural keys (email) as primary keys, then needing to change them.

notes.title: Denormalisation and when to break the rules
notes.html:
Denormalisation means copying data on purpose to avoid a join on a hot read path. You trade write complexity and storage for read speed.

Good reasons: a feed query joins 5 tables at 20,000 QPS; a counter like likes_count is read far more often than it changes; reporting tables. Bad reason: "joins are slow" with no measurement. Postgres joins on indexed keys are fast; the cost is usually in missing indexes.

Techniques: store a summary column (orders.item_count), a materialised view refreshed on schedule, a read-model table updated by a consumer from an event stream, or a cache.

Worked example. Order list screen needs customer name + item count + total. Joining 3 tables for 25 rows costs about 3 ms; at 10,000 QPS that is 30 cores busy. A denormalised order_summary row read by primary key costs about 0.3 ms.

Decision gravity. Reversible if the denormalised copy is derived and can be rebuilt from the source. One-way and dangerous if the copy becomes the only truth.

Industry examples. Twitter timelines are precomputed (fan-out on write). Instagram stores counters denormalised. Shopify keeps denormalised aggregates for dashboards.

Everyday analogy. Writing the total on the receipt instead of making the cashier re-add the items every time someone asks.

Common interview traps.

  • Denormalising without a plan for keeping copies in sync (drift bugs).
  • Counter columns updated on every like causing a hot row lock; batch or shard counters.

notes.title: Primary keys at scale
notes.html:
The primary key choice decides insert speed, index size and whether you can shard later.

Key type Pros Cons
Auto-increment BIGINT Small (8 B), sequential, cache friendly Single-node generator, leaks counts, hard when sharding
UUID v4 (random) Generate anywhere, no coordination 16 B, random inserts fragment the B-tree, poor cache locality
UUID v7 / ULID (time-ordered) Anywhere + roughly sequential 16 B, clock-dependent
Snowflake-style 64-bit ID 64-bit, time-ordered, no central DB Needs worker ID assignment, clock handling

A Snowflake ID packs about 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of machine ID and 12 bits of sequence: up to 4096 IDs per ms per machine.

| 1 sign | 41 bits timestamp ms | 10 bits worker | 12 bits sequence |

Why random UUIDs hurt: in a B-tree, each insert goes to a random leaf page. With a 100 GB index that does not fit in RAM, nearly every insert causes a disk read plus later page splits, wasting about 30 to 50 percent of space. Time-ordered keys always append to the rightmost leaf, which stays in memory.

Industry examples. Twitter invented Snowflake. Instagram generates 64-bit IDs inside Postgres with a shard ID, timestamp and per-shard sequence. Discord uses Snowflake-like IDs. Stripe uses prefixed random-ish string IDs (ch_...).

Decision gravity. One-way door. Changing the primary key after 1B rows means rewriting every table and every foreign key. Pick before launch.

Everyday analogy. Numbered tickets at a deli (sequential, easy to find) versus random raffle numbers scattered across a giant wall (hard to keep tidy).

Common interview traps.

  • Exposing sequential IDs publicly (enumeration attacks, business metric leak).
  • Random UUID primary key on a huge InnoDB table: InnoDB clusters rows by primary key, so it is worse there than in Postgres heap tables.
  • Using 32-bit INT: it overflows at about 2.1 billion rows; this is a classic production outage.

notes.title: Connection pooling with numbers
notes.html:
A database connection is expensive, so you keep a small pool and reuse it. In Postgres each connection is a separate OS process using roughly 5 to 10 MB of RAM (more with work_mem use), and performance falls when active connections far exceed CPU cores.

A rule of thumb from the HikariCP project: pool size = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count. For an 8-core DB server with SSDs, a pool of about 17 active connections total is often best, which surprises people.

Worked example. 50 app pods, each with a pool of 20 = 1,000 connections to Postgres. Postgres max_connections default is 100; raising to 1,000 costs about 5 to 10 GB RAM and slows everything via context switches. Fix: PgBouncer in transaction mode with default_pool_size = 40, max_client_conn = 5000. The database sees 40 connections, the apps see 5,000.

Little's Law helps sizing: connections needed = throughput x average query time. At 2,000 queries/s with 5 ms each: 2000 x 0.005 = 10 busy connections. So a pool of 20 is plenty; 200 is waste.

# pgbouncer.ini
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 40
max_client_conn = 5000
server_idle_timeout = 600
# HikariCP via Spring
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 20
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout: 3000   # ms to wait for a connection
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime: 1740000      # below DB/LB idle kill

Transaction-mode caveat: session features (prepared statements across transactions in older setups, SET, advisory locks, LISTEN) break because the next statement may run on a different server connection.

Incident pattern. Symptom: p99 latency jumps, app logs "timeout waiting for connection from pool", DB CPU low. Metrics: pool pending count rising, pg_stat_activity showing many idle in transaction. Cause: slow transactions holding connections or a leak.

Industry examples. Instagram, GitLab and many Rails shops use PgBouncer. AWS offers RDS Proxy for the same purpose, valuable with Lambda where thousands of short-lived functions would otherwise each open a connection.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen with 10 stoves and 200 cooks queueing; adding more cooks to the pile does not cook faster, it just makes the kitchen crowded.

Common interview traps.

  • Increasing pool size to fix slowness; it usually makes it worse.
  • Forgetting total connections = pods x pool size when autoscaling.
  • Holding a connection open while calling an external API.

notes.title: Indexes and query shape for scale
notes.html:
Most "SQL is slow" problems are missing or wrong indexes. An index is a sorted side structure that turns a full table scan (read 50M rows) into a lookup (read about 4 pages). Details are in the index notes; here the schema-level rules:

  • Index every foreign key and every column in frequent WHERE/ORDER BY.
  • Put equality columns first and range/sort columns last in composite indexes.
  • Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < :last ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 25) instead of OFFSET 1000000, which scans and discards a million rows.
  • Check with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
-- Slow at depth: scans and throws away 1,000,000 rows
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 25;
-- Fast: seeks directly
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id < 9000000 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 25;

Worked example. A table of 100M rows at 200 B is 20 GB. A full scan at 1 GB/s is 20 s. A B-tree with fan-out of about 300 has height 4, so lookup is about 4 page reads, around 1 ms when cached.

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a textbook versus reading every page to find "photosynthesis".

Common interview traps.

  • Too many indexes: each one slows every write and eats RAM.
  • Functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email)=...) without an expression index.
  • SELECT * defeating covering indexes.

notes.title: Scaling reads: replicas, caches, partitioning
notes.html:
The order of moves for a growing SQL database: tune queries and indexes, scale up, add a cache, add read replicas, partition big tables, and only then shard.

  • Read replicas: copy the primary's WAL stream. Reads go to replicas. Costs: replication lag (typically milliseconds, can be seconds under load), so "read your own write" needs care (route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write).
  • Table partitioning (within one DB): split events by month so old partitions can be dropped instantly and queries prune to one partition. Postgres declarative partitioning; keep partitions at a sensible count (hundreds, not tens of thousands).
  • Sharding (across DBs): split rows by a key (user_id hash) over several servers. Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard or impossible.

Worked example. 20,000 read QPS, 500 write QPS. A primary handles 500 writes easily; add 3 replicas each doing about 7,000 reads/s. Then a Redis cache with 90 percent hit rate cuts DB reads to 2,000/s, so one replica would do.

Decision gravity. Replicas and caches are reversible. Sharding is a one-way door: the shard key (user_id vs tenant_id) bakes into every query. Choose a key that keeps most queries on one shard and spreads load evenly.

Industry examples. Instagram shards Postgres by user. Shopify shards MySQL per shop. Notion sharded Postgres into 32 then 96 logical shards in their public engineering write-up (confirm figures in their blog). Vitess (YouTube) and Citus provide sharding layers.

Everyday analogy. A library adding photocopies of popular books (replicas) before building a second library across town (shards).

Common interview traps.

  • Reading from a lagging replica right after a write.
  • Sharding by an attribute that makes one shard hot (celebrity user, one huge tenant).
  • Promising cross-shard ACID transactions for free.

notes.title: Migrations and operating a big table
notes.html:
Changing the schema on a table with 500M rows is an operational risk, not a typing task. An ALTER TABLE can take a lock that blocks all writes.

Safe pattern ("expand and contract"):

  1. Add the new nullable column (fast in modern Postgres, metadata only).
  2. Deploy code that writes both old and new.
  3. Backfill in batches of 1,000 to 10,000 rows with sleeps.
  4. Switch reads to the new column.
  5. Drop the old column later.
-- Postgres: build index without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
-- Add constraint without a long lock
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_nonneg CHECK (total_cents >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_nonneg;

Incident pattern. Symptom: all writes hang right after a deploy. Metric: lock waits, pg_locks showing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request queued behind a long-running query, blocking everything behind it. Set lock_timeout = '3s' on migrations so they fail fast.

Industry examples. GitHub's gh-ost and Percona's pt-online-schema-change do online MySQL schema changes by copying into a shadow table; Postgres teams use pg_repack and careful concurrent operations.

Everyday analogy. Renovating a shop while customers keep shopping: you build the new shelf beside the old one and move stock over, rather than closing the doors.

Common interview traps.

  • Running ALTER inside a migration with no lock_timeout.
  • Backfilling with one giant UPDATE that bloats WAL and locks rows.
  • Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it (old pods still running).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• SQL is the default store for anything needing multi-row correctness and flexible queries; one good node goes very far.
  • Normalise the source of truth; denormalise only derived read copies you can rebuild.
  • Primary key is a one-way door: prefer 64-bit time-ordered IDs; avoid random UUIDs on huge clustered tables; never use 32-bit counters for big tables.
  • Pool connections small: about cores x 2 per DB, use PgBouncer; total connections = pods x pool size; Little's Law sizes it.
  • Scale in order: indexes, scale up, cache, replicas (watch lag), partitioning, sharding last.
  • Migrate with expand and contract, CONCURRENTLY, batch backfills and lock_timeout.

questions.subtopic: When SQL is the right choice
questions.promptHtml: When would you pick a relational database for a new system, and when would you not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The first decision in any design; checks that you choose from access patterns and numbers, not fashion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I choose SQL when I need correctness across several rows or tables, flexible queries, or I do not yet know the future queries: payments, orders, bookings, inventory, accounts. One good Postgres or MySQL node does about 20,000 to 50,000 indexed reads/s and 5,000 to 15,000 transactional writes/s (benchmark it), far more than most products need. I look elsewhere for giant append-only streams (millions of writes/s), pure key lookups at huge QPS (Redis), or deep graph traversals.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The planner turns declarative SQL into an access path, so new queries need no new data model. Constraints (foreign keys, checks) and multi-row ACID transactions protect invariants.

Need SQL? Why
Transfer money between accounts Yes Multi-row transaction
Ad-hoc reports, joins Yes Planner handles unknown queries
1M sensor writes/s Not alone Single-node write ceiling
Session lookup 500k/s Overkill Redis cheaper per op
Friends of friends, depth 5 Poor Self-join explosion

A shop with 5M orders a year is 0.16 orders/s, nowhere near any limit. Primary store choice is close to a one-way door (moving 2 TB live takes months); adding cache or search later is reversible because they are derived copies.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "SQL does not scale." Single-node SQL scales a lot; sharding is a late step.
  • NoSQL "because scale" with no number.
  • SQL as a queue (polling status='NEW').
  • Blobs in rows instead of object storage.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would make you leave SQL? -> A measured write rate beyond one primary, or a pattern like deep graph hops.
  2. How do you add a search box later? -> Derived Elasticsearch index fed by CDC; SQL stays the source of truth.
  3. Why is the choice a one-way door? -> Migration needs dual writes, backfill and verification over months.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "SQL for structured data, NoSQL for scale." Senior: states the numbers, names the one-way door, keeps one system of record, derives the rest.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup moved to a document store "for scale" at 100 writes/s, then rebuilt joins in application code and reporting by hand.

questions.promptHtml: What primary key would you use for a table expected to reach billions of rows, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The key decides insert speed, index size and whether sharding is possible; it is hard to change later.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A 64-bit, roughly time-ordered ID: BIGINT identity if a single database generates it, or a Snowflake-style or UUIDv7 ID if multiple writers or shards need to generate without coordination. I avoid random UUIDv4 as the clustered key on a huge table because every insert lands on a random page; I never use 32-bit INT for growing tables (overflow at about 2.1B rows). I do not expose sequential IDs publicly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key Pros Cons
BIGINT identity 8 B, sequential Single generator, leaks counts
UUIDv4 Generate anywhere 16 B, random inserts fragment the B-tree
UUIDv7/ULID Anywhere, time-ordered 16 B, clock dependent
Snowflake 64-bit, time-ordered Needs worker ids and clock handling 
| 1 sign | 41 bits ms timestamp | 10 bits worker | 12 bits sequence |   4096 ids/ms/worker

Why random hurts: with a 100 GB index not fitting in RAM, nearly every insert reads a random leaf from disk and splits pages, wasting 30 to 50% of space. Time-ordered keys append to the rightmost leaf, which stays cached. In InnoDB rows are clustered by primary key, so random UUIDs are worse than in Postgres heap tables.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• INT overflow: a classic outage.
  • Natural keys like email that later change.
  • Sequential ids exposed publicly (enumeration, metric leak).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Public IDs with a sequential key? -> Keep an internal BIGINT PK and a separate random public id, or encode.
  2. Clock moves backward in Snowflake? -> Wait or refuse until time catches up; never reuse.
  3. Sharding later? -> Embed a shard id in the ID (as Instagram's scheme does) so the key routes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "UUID so it scales". Senior: explains B-tree locality, clustered vs heap, and the one-way door.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 32-bit identity column on an events table reached 2^31 and writes failed at 3 a.m.

questions.contextHtml:
At 02:14 an e-commerce platform starts failing every order insert:

ERROR: integer out of range
DETAIL: nextval: reached maximum value of sequence "order_events_id_seq" (2147483647)

order_events has 2.1B rows and 900 GB, grows 30M rows/day, and is written by 12 services. A hotfix must be live before the 09:00 peak. Replication to two replicas is healthy; CPU is 20%.
questions.promptHtml: Stop the bleeding and plan the real fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ALTER COLUMN TYPE BIGINT now." That rewrites 900 GB under an exclusive lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do other tables reference this id (foreign keys)? Are old rows needed online? Can writers tolerate gaps or a negative id range? Is there a partitioned layout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Sequences are signed; restart at a new range: ALTER SEQUENCE ... MINVALUE -2147483648 RESTART WITH -2147483648 so ids run through the negative half (about 2.1B more values) if the column is INT, buying about 70 days at 30M/day. Check consumers that assume positive ids first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pure overflow of INT identity; no other cause (red herring: CPU, replication).
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT last_value FROM order_events_id_seq, check column types of referencing tables, grep services for ids stored in int32 (including Java int and mobile clients).
  5. Root cause: 32-bit key on a table that grows by tens of millions of rows per day.
  6. Fix: Long term: create order_events_new with BIGINT, dual write, backfill in batches of 10,000, swap by rename in a short lock with lock_timeout, and update every FK and client type; for a partitioned table migrate partition by partition. Consider archiving old data.
  7. Prevention: Alert when any sequence passes 50% of its type range; schema lint forbidding INT ids; capacity review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not an in-place ALTER TYPE on 900 GB during business hours. The negative range is a temporary hack that can break systems assuming positive ids.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Downstream Kafka schema has int? -> Version the schema; ids must be int64 everywhere.
  • Mobile clients parse as int32? -> JSON big values overflow; ship client updates or send ids as strings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An id sequence alert at 80% had been silenced as noise two years earlier; the overflow was found at 2 a.m. by the on-call.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Runs ALTER in place.
  • Hire: Temporary range trick and shadow-table migration.
  • Strong hire: FK, client and schema impact, alerting and sequence-range monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
Postgres on 16 vCPU, max_connections = 1000 raised last month. 60 app pods autoscale; each has a Hikari pool of maximum-pool-size: 30. During a sale the HPA scales to 60 pods. Symptoms:

p99 latency 80 ms -> 2.4 s
pg_stat_activity: 1,620 connections requested, 1000 max -> "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already"
CPU 100%, load average 70, context switches 600k/s
app log: HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 3000ms
queries avg 6 ms, QPS 3,000
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what is the right pool design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise max_connections and pool size more."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Any long transactions or idle in transaction? Do pods call external APIs while holding a connection? Which pool mode can the ORM tolerate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap HPA max pods or reduce each pool to 10; deploy PgBouncer in transaction mode.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Total connections = pods x pool = 60 x 30 = 1,800 > 1,000; too many active connections on 16 cores causes context-switch thrash; slow transactions hold connections.
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY 1;, idle in transaction age, Hikari metrics (pending, active).
  5. Root cause: Connections beyond about 2 x cores add contention, not throughput. Little's Law: needed busy connections = 3,000 QPS x 0.006 s = 18. A pool of 1,800 is 100x oversized.
  6. Fix:
# pgbouncer.ini
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 40
max_client_conn = 5000
server_idle_timeout = 600
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout: 3000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime: 1740000

The DB sees about 40 connections; the apps see up to 5,000 client connections. 7. Prevention: Alert on connections / max_connections > 70%, enforce pods x pool in capacity review, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Transaction mode breaks session state (SET, advisory locks, LISTEN, some prepared statements); test the ORM. Not raise max_connections (5 to 10 MB per backend and scheduler thrash).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lambda functions? -> RDS Proxy or PgBouncer, since thousands of short-lived functions would each open a connection.
  • Latency is still high at 40 connections? -> Then the queries are slow (indexes, locks), not the pool.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Doubling a pool to "fix" timeouts doubled load average and made timeouts worse; reducing it to 12 restored p99.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raises pool and limit.
  • Hire: Multiplies pods x pool, uses PgBouncer.
  • Strong hire: Little's Law, transaction-mode caveats, alerts and cause analysis of idle in transaction.

questions.contextHtml:
A support console lists orders for a customer. With 120M rows the page "load more" gets slower the deeper you go (page 400 takes 9 s). Search by email also seems slow. Code and plan:

-- list
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 20000 LIMIT 25;

-- search
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com';
Limit  (cost=...) (actual time=8870..8870 rows=25)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=8210..8700 rows=20025)
        ->  Seq Scan on orders  Filter: (customer_id = 42)  Rows Removed by Filter: 119,979,975
Seq Scan on customers (actual time=1900 ms)
Indexes: orders_pkey, customers_pkey, customers_email_key (email)

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM" or "index everything".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is customer_id indexed? Do users need random page jump or only "next"? Is email stored case-sensitively? Which columns does the page actually show?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No index matching filter and sort (Seq Scan then Sort of 20,025 rows); OFFSET scans and discards 20,000 rows; lower(email) cannot use the plain email index; SELECT * blocks index-only scans.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after; check pg_stat_user_indexes.
  5. Root cause: Equality column first, sort column next is missing from the index; OFFSET is O(offset); function on indexed column.
  6. Fix:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);
-- keyset pagination
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND (created_at, id) < (:last_created, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 25;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY customers_email_lower ON customers (lower(email));

Return a cursor, not page numbers. 7. Prevention: Slow query log with EXPLAIN review on PRs; lint for OFFSET above a threshold. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Each index slows writes and uses RAM; no blanket indexing. Cursor pagination cannot jump to page 400; for support UIs that is acceptable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two orders with the same created_at? -> The tiebreaker id in the cursor.
  • Table 10x bigger? -> Same lookup cost; B-tree depth grows by about one level (fan-out about 300).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An export job paging with OFFSET took 6 hours; keyset paging made it 12 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds hardware.
  • Hire: Composite index and keyset pagination.
  • Strong hire: Expression index, tiebreaker, covering columns, write-cost trade-off.

questions.contextHtml:
Reads were moved to 2 replicas to relieve the primary (20,000 read QPS, 500 write QPS). Since then support gets tickets: "I updated my address and the page shows the old one", and sometimes an order disappears from "My orders" for a few seconds after checkout. Metrics:

replica_lag_seconds: p50 0.04  p99 3.8  max 21 (during nightly batch)
primary CPU: 70% -> 25%
error rate: none
questions.promptHtml: Why does this happen and how do you fix it without giving up the replicas?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replication is broken", or "send everything to the primary again".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is replication async? Which reads must be fresh (own writes) and which can be stale? Is there a proxy that routes reads?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route reads of the writing user to the primary for a short window after a write, or for sensitive screens.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Asynchronous replication lag (p99 3.8 s); nightly batch makes lag worse; load balancing across replicas of different lag gives inconsistent views (user sees new, then old).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_replication lag per replica, correlate ticket timestamps with lag spikes.
  5. Root cause: Read-your-writes is not guaranteed on async replicas.
  6. Fix: After a write, store the commit LSN or timestamp in the session; a read goes to a replica only if replay_lsn >= that LSN, else to the primary; or pin the user to the primary for 5 s. Keep an explicit class of "must be fresh" queries. Reduce lag: throttle batch jobs, separate replica for reporting.
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();           -- on primary after commit
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn();       -- on replica, compare
  1. Prevention: Alert when lag p99 exceeds 1 s; test hooks that inject lag in staging.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Synchronous replication removes staleness but raises write latency and risks availability. Do not read money or inventory from replicas to make decisions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Monotonic reads? -> Pin a session to one replica so it never goes back in time.
  • Failover while lagging? -> Writes confirmed on the old primary but not replicated can be lost; know your RPO.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly index rebuild raised lag to 20 s and the next morning's "my payment is missing" tickets all came from the same 6-minute window.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Everything back to primary.
  • Hire: Read-your-writes routing for recent writers.
  • Strong hire: LSN-based routing, lag alerts, monotonic reads, failover RPO.

questions.promptHtml: When do you normalise and when do you deliberately denormalise?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you treat denormalisation as a measured trade-off with a sync plan, not a reflex.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I normalise the source of truth to about 3NF so each fact lives once: no duplicated addresses, no update anomalies. I denormalise only a derived read copy for a measured hot path: a summary column, a materialised view or a read-model table fed by a change stream. The source stays normalised and the copy can be rebuilt; if the copy becomes the only truth, it is dangerous.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Normal forms in plain words: 1NF one value per cell; 2NF non-key columns depend on the whole key; 3NF non-key columns depend only on the key.

Good reasons to denormalise: a feed joining 5 tables at 20,000 QPS, counters read far more often than written, reporting. Bad reason: "joins are slow" without measurement (indexed joins are fast; the usual culprit is a missing index).

Numbers: an order list joining 3 tables for 25 rows is about 3 ms; at 10,000 QPS that is 30 cores. A read table order_summary by primary key is about 0.3 ms.

Write API -> normalised tables -> change stream -> denormalised read table
Read API  -> denormalised read table

Keep copies in sync with transactions (same DB), triggers (careful), or CDC/outbox events (cross DB), and add a reconciliation job that recomputes and compares.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No plan for drift between copies.
  • Counter columns updated on every event cause a hot row.
  • Storing JSON arrays then querying inside constantly.
  • Floats for money; natural keys that change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect drift? -> Periodic recompute-and-diff job with an alert.
  2. Materialised view refresh cost? -> Full refresh scans everything; use incremental tables or REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking reads.
  3. Is it a one-way door? -> No if derived and rebuildable; yes if it is the only copy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "denormalise for speed". Senior: measures first, names the sync mechanism, keeps the source of truth normalised, adds reconciliation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A denormalised customer_name on orders diverged after a rename import; invoices went out with two spellings.

questions.promptHtml: How do you change the schema of a table with 500M rows while serving production traffic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Schema changes are operational risks; this separates people who have caused a lock outage from those who have not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use expand and contract so every deploy is backward compatible: add the new nullable column (metadata only), deploy code that writes both, backfill in small batches with pauses, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release. I build indexes with CONCURRENTLY, add constraints as NOT VALID then VALIDATE, and set lock_timeout so a migration fails fast instead of queuing behind a long query and blocking everyone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Add column -> Dual write -> Backfill (1k-10k rows/batch) -> Switch reads -> Drop old (next release)
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_nonneg CHECK (total_cents >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_nonneg;   -- scans without a long exclusive lock

Why locks cascade: an ALTER needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; it waits behind a long query; every new query then waits behind the ALTER, so the table is effectively down. Backfills as one UPDATE bloat WAL, create replica lag and hold row locks. Old pods are still running during a rollout, so dropping a column in the same release that stops using it breaks them. MySQL tools: gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change (shadow table copy).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No lock_timeout.
  • One giant backfill UPDATE.
  • Drop in the same deploy.
  • Adding a column with a volatile default on an old Postgres version (rewrite; verify for your version).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Renaming a column? -> Add new, dual write, backfill, switch, drop; never RENAME while old code runs.
  2. How do you throttle a backfill? -> Batch size, sleep, watch replica lag and stop when it rises.
  3. Rollback plan? -> Keep the old column until the new path is proven; each step is reversible.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "run the ALTER at night". Senior: lock queue behavior, batching, compatibility across versions, replica lag.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "quick" ALTER queued behind a 20-minute report query and froze all writes for 12 minutes.

questions.contextHtml:
14:02 a deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN gift_note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''; on a 500M row Postgres table. At 14:03 writes hang.

pg_stat_activity:
 pid 811  state=active   query='SELECT ... FROM orders ...' (running 14 min, analytics)
 pid 904  state=active   wait_event=Lock  query='ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ...'
 pids 1,100+ state=active wait_event=Lock  query='INSERT INTO orders ...'
API 5xx: 41%   pool timeouts rising   DB CPU 8%

The team asks to kill the migration, then wants to retry it.
questions.promptHtml: Handle the incident and design the retry.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the database." It loses in-flight work and the same lock pile-up returns.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Postgres version (fast defaults vs rewrite)? Can we kill the analytics query? Is the migration transactional?
  2. Immediate mitigation: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(904); to cancel the ALTER (the queued inserts then proceed); consider cancelling the analytics query too if safe.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ALTER waiting for ACCESS EXCLUSIVE behind a 14-minute query, blocking every later statement (low CPU, many Lock waits confirm); not a CPU or capacity issue (red herring: 8% CPU).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_blocking_pids() and pg_locks to see the chain.
  5. Root cause: No lock_timeout and a long-running reader.
  6. Fix: Retry with SET lock_timeout = '3s' in a loop with backoff, at a quiet time, after analytics moved to a replica. In modern Postgres, ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT constant is metadata-only (verify version); NOT NULL with a default is also fast then. For older versions or a heavy change use add nullable, backfill in batches, then SET NOT NULL via validated check.
  7. Prevention: Migration runner forces lock_timeout and statement_timeout, blocks migrations when long queries exist, run analytics only on replicas.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not restart the DB. Fail-fast retries risk never succeeding on a busy table; schedule a window or use a shadow-table tool.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The ALTER already ran halfway? -> Postgres DDL is transactional; cancel rolls back.
  • MySQL? -> Use online DDL options or gh-ost; check metadata lock waits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reporting query left in a notebook for an hour blocked a 2-second migration and froze checkout; lock_timeout became a deploy gate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Restart DB.
  • Hire: Finds the blocker and cancels, retries with lock_timeout.
  • Strong hire: Lock queue explanation, replica for analytics, version-aware fast default, pipeline guard.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app stores posts.likes_count and increments it with UPDATE posts SET likes_count = likes_count + 1 WHERE id = :id on every like. A celebrity post goes viral: 4,000 likes/s on one row.

pg_stat_activity: 380 sessions waiting  wait_event_type=Lock (transactionid)
tps overall: 9,000 -> 1,100
p99 like API: 4.8 s
dead tuples on posts: 2.1M and rising, autovacuum busy
CPU 35%

Other posts are fine. Product wants the count to be "roughly right, within seconds".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the connection pool."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the count be exact? Do we need per-user dedupe (one like per user)? Is the count shown on the feed at 100k QPS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move increments off the row: buffer them (Redis INCR or an in-app batch) and flush every second.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Row lock contention: each UPDATE takes a row lock until commit so updates serialize; MVCC creates a dead tuple per update, bloating the table; the pool is a victim, not the cause.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_locks grouped by relation and tuple, pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup.
  5. Root cause: A single hot row serializes writers.
  6. Fix: Insert likes into a likes(post_id, user_id) table with a unique key (dedupe) and keep the displayed count as a derived value: either sharded counters (post_id, shard 0..15, sum on read) or a batched flush every 1 s adding the delta once. Rebuild periodically from the likes table.
INSERT INTO like_counters (post_id, shard, n) VALUES (:p, :s, 1)
ON CONFLICT (post_id, shard) DO UPDATE SET n = like_counters.n + 1;
SELECT sum(n) FROM like_counters WHERE post_id = :p;
  1. Prevention: Hot-row alert (lock waits by key), load test with skew rather than uniform ids.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The displayed count may lag a second; the likes table remains the truth. Do not make the counter the only record (it cannot be rebuilt or deduped).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same issue on inventory? -> Different: it needs exactness; use reservations or a queue per SKU.
  • Why sharded counters over Redis only? -> Redis can lose recent counts on failover; fine as a buffer, reconcile from the table.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day product page counter hit one row at 1,500/s; moving to 16 shard rows restored throughput with no visible change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More connections.
  • Hire: Row lock diagnosis, shard or batch counter.
  • Strong hire: Dedupe table as truth, reconciliation, bloat analysis, exactness trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B SaaS has one Postgres primary (32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, 8 TB, 3 replicas). Growth is 15% per month. Today: writes 4,000/s (limit tested at about 9,000), reads 25,000/s served mostly by replicas, buffer cache hit ratio 93% and falling, vacuum struggling on two 2 TB tables. A principal engineer proposes sharding by user_id now. Customers are companies with 1 to 50,000 users; a few big tenants make 40% of traffic. Many queries join across a tenant's users.
questions.promptHtml: Do you shard now? What do you do, and what shard key?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, shard by user_id for scale."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual bottleneck: write throughput, working set, vacuum, or storage? Growth projection to 12 months? Cross-tenant queries? Can the big tenants be isolated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheaper steps first: tune queries and indexes, partition the two 2 TB tables by time (drop old partitions), archive cold data, raise RAM to fit the working set, add a cache for hot reads.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Working set no longer fits RAM (cache hit 93% falling); vacuum and bloat on big tables; writes at 44% of tested ceiling are not the constraint yet.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_statements top queries by total time, per-table size and bloat, cache hit by table, write IOPS headroom.
  5. Root cause: Growth is eating memory and maintenance windows, not write capacity.
  6. Fix: Ladder: indexes, scale up, cache, replicas, partitioning, then shard. If sharding becomes necessary, shard by tenant_id (not user_id): tenant queries stay on one shard and joins within a tenant remain local; place the few giant tenants on dedicated shards; use a tenant-to-shard directory so tenants can move. Evaluate Citus or Vitess-style layers (confirm fit) rather than hand-rolling.
  7. Prevention: Capacity forecast with triggers (for example write p95 at 60% of tested ceiling or DB over 12 TB), keep ids shard-aware (shard id in the key).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharding is a one-way door: shard key bakes into every query; cross-shard joins and transactions are hard or gone. Do not shard before the cheaper steps are exhausted.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A tenant outgrows a shard? -> Directory-based mapping lets you move it with dual write and cutover.
  • Global reports across tenants? -> Replicate to a warehouse; do not join across shards online.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sharded by user at 2 TB, then discovered every product screen joined across users of an org; a year later they were rebuilding by tenant.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Shards immediately by user_id.
  • Hire: Climbs the ladder, identifies tenant key.
  • Strong hire: Evidence-based bottleneck analysis, directory, hot-tenant isolation, triggers.

questions.subtopic: Schema choice for a new product
questions.contextHtml: A founder says: "We are building a marketplace. We will have millions of users, so we need a scalable database; the CTO says use MongoDB. Launch in 3 months." You learn: orders and payments with refunds, sellers with inventory counts, buyer search with filters, and a reporting need from finance. Expected year-one numbers: 200k users, 2,000 orders/day, 50 writes/s peak.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask and what do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts MongoDB "for scale" or declares SQL "obviously" without numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the top 5 queries and their QPS? Do refunds and inventory require multi-row consistency? What staleness can search tolerate? What does the team already operate? What is the 3-year growth?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would start with a decision record, not a product name.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The data is relational (users, orders, items, payments, refunds); money and stock need transactions; reporting needs joins; load is tiny (50 writes/s is less than 1% of a single node).
  4. How I'd verify: Back-of-envelope: 2,000 orders/day is 0.02 per second; even 100x growth is 2/s. One Postgres primary covers it by orders of magnitude; run a load test with 10x data.
  5. Root cause of the decision: The need is correctness and flexible queries, not horizontal write scale.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Postgres as the single system of record, normalised, BIGINT/time-ordered ids, integer cents, FKs and indexes. Add Redis for sessions and cache, and Elasticsearch/OpenSearch fed by CDC for search later if needed. Object storage for images. Read replicas when reads need them. Document the trigger conditions for revisiting (write rate, size).
  7. Prevention: Keep derived stores rebuildable; name the system of record; schedule a capacity review per quarter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: MongoDB is plausible for the catalogue but splitting orders across engines adds failure modes with no scale benefit at this size. The primary store is the one-way door; a cache or index is a two-way door. Honor the CTO by treating a document store for flexible product attributes as an option once there is a measured need, or use JSONB columns.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Founder insists on "millions of users"? -> Show that users do not equal writes; revisit at measured thresholds.
  • Product attributes vary a lot? -> JSONB with a GIN index for the variable part, relational for the core.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A seed-stage team picked a distributed document store for a "scalable" launch, then built ad-hoc transactions and reporting exports for a year before migrating to Postgres.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Agrees to either choice without questions.
  • Hire: Asks access patterns, computes load, chooses SQL.
  • Strong hire: Names one-way vs two-way doors, trigger criteria, JSONB for flexibility, respects the CTO's concerns.
